[IMAGE] This image illustrates the concept of the "Money Multiplier" or "Deposit Creation" by commercial banks in the banking system. The sketch represents how an initial deposit (shown by the first hand placing money) gets fractionally reserved by banks and then lent out to others (depicted by the subsequent hands), thereby creating additional deposits in the economy.

The interconnected hands symbolize the process of multiple deposit creation, where each new deposit leads to further lending and deposit generation, thus expanding the money supply beyond the original amount deposited. The bricks at the top likely represent the initial cash reserve that banks hold.

title: NCERT Grade 12 Economics | Image | Page 1
text:
[IMAGE] This image appears to illustrate the concept of Circular Flow of Income in a simple economy, often discussed in introductory economics.

The diagram shows the interaction between two key economic agents: households and firms. The labeled parts typically represent the flow of goods and services (from firms to households) and the corresponding flow of factor payments (like wages, rent, interest, and profits) from firms to households in return for the factors of production (like labor and capital). The circular arrows indicate the continuous and interdependent exchange that sustains economic activity.
Source: NCERT Grade 12 Economics, Page 1

title: NCERT Grade 12 Economics | Image | Page 17
text:
[IMAGE] This image illustrates the concept of profit repatriation in an open economy, highlighting the flow of profits from domestic economic activities to foreigners.

The labeled parts include the "Domestic Economy," represented by a car, which signifies businesses or industries operating within a country, and "Foreigners," who are depicted as receiving entities. The image shows the process where profits, generated by foreign-owned businesses operating within the domestic economy, are sent back (repatriated) to the foreign investors or owners. This demonstrates how foreign direct investment can lead to an outflow of profits from the domestic economy to foreign entities.
Source: NCERT Grade 12 Economics, Page 17

title: NCERT Grade 12 Economics | Image | Page 9
text:
[IMAGE] This image appears to be a simple graphical representation of a Production Possibilities Curve (PPC) or Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), a fundamental concept in Economics.

The PPC illustrates the different combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with its existing resources and technology when all resources are fully and efficiently utilized. The curve typically shows the trade-offs between producing two goods, highlighting the concept of opportunity cost. The axes are generally labeled with the quantities of the two goods, such as "Good X" and "Good Y."
Source: NCERT Grade 12 Economics, Page 9

title: NCERT Grade 12 Economics | Image | Page 1
text:
[IMAGE] This image illustrates the concept of a "Production Possibilities Curve" (PPC) or Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF), which is a fundamental topic in microeconomics.

The diagram shows the maximum potential output combinations of two goods that an economy can achieve by efficiently utilizing its available resources and technology. The shaded blue area represents the attainable but inefficient use of resources, while the curved line itself indicates the efficient production frontier where resources are fully utilized. The axes typically represent quantities of two different goods or services.
Source: NCERT Grade 12 Economics, Page 1

[IMAGE] This image illustrates the concept of progressive taxation, a key topic in economics.

The diagram shows a person struggling to climb a set of stairs labeled "Taxes," where each step gets progressively taller. This visually represents how the tax rate increases as the taxable income increases, meaning individuals pay a higher percentage of tax on larger portions of their income. The increasing difficulty in climbing each step symbolizes the rising burden of taxes with higher income levels.
Source: NCERT Grade 12 Economics, Page 10
